S009: Six loose counters arrive|at two trays marked with the same letter.|Split them equally.|Three on this tray and three on its twin.|A digit written twice must describe|the same quantity both times.

Now each tray holds a two digit number|ending in five.|Together their total begins with seven.|Tip the two groups of five into the units drawer.|All ten fit in a sleeve worth one ten.|The units drawer is empty.|Its digit is zero.

The tens drawer shows seven sleeves.|One just came across from the units.|Take that one aside.|Six sleeves remain,|shared equally by the two trays.|Each tray supplied three tens.|Thirty five and thirty five make seventy.

Turn the counter round.|Two copies of the number A B|have made a three digit total labelled B C D.|Different letters must have different digits.|We want the smallest possible A B.|Before opening the drawers,|which letter can you name?

Even ninety nine doubled|is only one hundred and ninety eight.|The hundreds drawer must hold exactly one,|so B is one.|Move that digit back to both units places.|One plus one leaves two units|and sends nothing into the tens.|D is two.

Four tens on each tray|would make only eight tens.|Five on each tray make ten tens.|Exchange them for one hundred.|No tens remain, so C is zero.|Read the finished drawers:|fifty one plus fifty one equals|one hundred and two.|Five, one, zero and two are all different.|No smaller tens digit can work.

Now double sixty eight.|Eight and eight make sixteen.|Leave six in the units drawer|and send one ten across.|Six tens and six tens plus the carried ten|make thirteen tens.|Exchange ten of those tens for a hundred.|The drawers read one hundred and thirty six.|In a letter sum, keep the digit you write|separate from the amount you carry.
S010: A ticket printer puts the same digit in two boxes.|Together those digits add to eight,|so each box shows four.|Turning that ticket would change nothing.|What changes when a ticket carries|two different digits?

Slide the larger digit from units to tens.|Each extra unit of digit difference|now gains ten in one place|and loses one in the other.|The net gain is nine.|A reversal that gains thirty six|therefore moves a digit four larger|into the tens place.

Our two digits also add to eight.|Set four counters aside for the difference.|The four left split into two matching pairs.|The smaller digit is two and the larger is six.|Print twenty six, then reverse it.|Sixty two minus twenty six is thirty six.

Inspect a different pair of tickets.|A B plus A C ends in zero,|with hundreds digit B and tens digit D.|All four letters use different digits.|Find the smallest A B.|Two two digit numbers cannot reach two hundred,|so the new hundreds digit is one.|B is one.

One plus C must end in zero.|Only nine can complete the ten.|Carry one.|The tens total is twice A plus one.|Four would give only nine,|so the first candidate is five.|Fifty one plus fifty nine equals|one hundred and ten.|Look at the hundreds and tens.|Two different letters would both be one.|Reject that ticket.

Move up one tens digit to six.|Sixty one plus sixty nine|makes one hundred and thirty.|Read the four letters in order:|six, one, nine, three.|None collides.|We have checked the only smaller candidate|that could reach a hundred.|The smallest legal first ticket is sixty one.

A fresh ticket gains twenty seven|when you reverse its digits.|The digits add to eleven.|What is the ticket?|Divide the gain by nine.|The digits differ by three.|Set three aside from eleven,|then halve the eight left.|The smaller digit is four, the larger seven.|Check the journey:|seventy four minus forty seven|equals twenty seven.|The ticket gaining value starts|with the smaller digit.
